sections.section: How did massive galaxies build their structure and kinematics at cosmic noon? Disk settling, dispersion support, and the inner dark-matter budget

claims.text: A large fraction of resolved, massive star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon (z about 1-3) are rotation-dominated but turbulent disks in emission-line integral-field data, rather than a population dominated by ongoing major mergers.

Intrinsic ionized-gas velocity dispersions in these disks are elevated at high redshift and decline toward the present, from about 50 km/s at z about 2.3 to about 25 km/s at z about 0.9 in mass-selected KMOS3D samples after beam-smearing and rotation are forward-modeled out.

At fixed stellar mass, star-forming galaxies are more compact at higher redshift, with rest-optical effective radius scaling roughly as (1+z)^-0.75 for late types and more steeply, about (1+z)^-1.48, for quiescent galaxies over 0 < z < 3.

In dynamical models the inner regions (within roughly one effective radius) of many massive cosmic-noon disks are baryon-dominated, with low inferred central dark-matter fractions, for example a median enclosed dark-matter fraction near 8 percent for a Chabrier IMF in z about 2 MOSDEF samples.

Whether most massive main-sequence galaxies at cosmic noon are already dynamically settled rotating disks or whether disturbed, dispersion-dominated, and merging systems remain a major channel is unresolved, because kinematic classification, resolution, depth, inclination, and pair-timescale assumptions prevent a selection-complete disk-versus-merger fraction across mass and redshift.
claims.debate_topic: Rotation-versus-dispersion support and the timing of disk settling

claims.text: Whether the low inferred inner dark-matter fractions of cosmic-noon disks reflect genuinely baryon-dominated centers or are partly an artifact of pressure support, IMF and gas-mass assumptions, and halo contraction versus cores is unresolved, because rotation curves rarely extend far beyond the luminous disk and the mass components are strongly degenerate.
claims.debate_topic: Baryon dominance versus modeling bias in inner dark-matter fractions

claims.text: Whether present-day massive galaxies quench through an early phase of central compaction into a dense star-forming core, or through gradual inside-out disk growth with progressive bulge buildup, is unresolved because cross-sectional populations and dust-sensitive resolved SEDs cannot uniquely reconstruct individual evolutionary tracks.
claims.debate_topic: Central compaction versus inside-out growth toward quiescence

claims.text: Whether the kiloparsec-scale clumps seen in gas-rich high-redshift disks are intrinsic, long-lived, in-situ structures formed by violent disk instability that migrate inward to build bulges, or are largely short-lived, feedback-disrupted, and inflated in mass by PSF blending and SED assumptions, is unresolved because clump ages, masses, and radial gradients are strongly resolution- and model-dependent.
claims.debate_topic: Clump longevity, migration, and measurement inflation

claims.text: Whether the star-forming main sequence at cosmic noon is near-linear or bends and flattens at the high-mass end, and how its normalization evolves, remains contested because SFR indicators, dust corrections, IMF, stacking, and bulge contamination shift the fitted slope and zero-point.

sections.section: Can we trust the stellar masses, ages, and star-formation rates we infer? Stellar-population-synthesis systematics

claims.text: A stellar-population-synthesis prediction combines an assumed initial mass function, stellar-evolution isochrones, and stellar spectra to build simple stellar populations, then convolves them with a star-formation history, enrichment, and dust for composite populations, so every inferred galaxy property inherits the adopted ingredients and priors and is not a direct observation.

Stellar mass is among the more robust SED-derived galaxy properties given adequate wavelength coverage and normal star-formation histories, but it remains an SPS-dependent mass-to-light scaling whose absolute value is set by the IMF and hidden old populations.

Old-population optical colors and many absorption indices suffer a strong age-metallicity degeneracy, approximately the Worthey 3/2 rule in which a factor-three change in age mimics a factor-two change in metallicity, most severe for populations older than about 5 Gyr with limited optical information.

The low-mass normalization of the IMF strongly controls stellar mass-to-light ratios while contributing little integrated light, so that roughly 60-80 percent of the stellar mass of an old population can reside in low-mass stars that are nearly invisible in optical and near-infrared SEDs.

Ultraviolet, recombination-line, and infrared star-formation-rate indicators average star formation over different timescales and dust sensitivities, with the UV continuum tracing roughly 100 Myr and Halpha recombination tracing less than about 10 Myr, and every calibration assumes an IMF, metallicity, SFH duration, and dust decomposition.

Whether the IMF is universal and Milky-Way-like or varies systematically with galaxy velocity dispersion or abundance is unresolved, with gravity-sensitive spectra, dynamics, and lensing by 2013 indicating that massive early-type galaxies may have heavier IMF normalizations, but abundance-response, dark-matter, and dynamical-modeling degeneracies prevent proof of a single universal trend.
claims.debate_topic: IMF universality and its effect on stellar masses

claims.text: Whether absolute stellar masses are accurate to about a factor of two or are limited by larger SPS, IMF, and SFH systematics is disputed, because formal fit errors of order 0.3 dex omit model mismatch and unseen old or low-mass populations, and extreme star-formation-history choices alone can shift recovered mass by up to about 0.6 dex.

Whether simple parametric star-formation histories such as exponential or rising models or flexible nonparametric, burst-capable reconstructions better recover mass, age, and past SFR is unresolved, because flexible models reduce bias but increase prior dependence and covariance between time bins, and young stars outshine older mass.

The strength of the thermally pulsing asymptotic-giant-branch contribution drives large near-infrared differences between SPS models for intermediate-age populations of roughly 0.1-2 Gyr, and whether the heavier or lighter prescriptions are correct is contested because cluster calibrators, stochasticity, metallicity, SFH, and circumstellar dust permit competing fits.

Whether a universal foreground-like attenuation law can be applied or whether effective attenuation varies with mixed star-dust geometry and stellar age is unresolved, because extinction and attenuation laws are not interchangeable and UV slope, IRX, inclination, and grain composition covary.

Whether optical spectra alone suffice to constrain a population or whether panchromatic UV-to-infrared energy-balance data are required is contested, because adding bands supplies information on young and dust-obscured stars but also introduces additional model systematics, and dust emission cannot be inferred from optical-only fits.

sections.section: How do galaxies connect to their dark-matter halos? Abundance matching, scatter, and assembly bias

claims.text: The central-galaxy stellar-to-halo mass relation is strongly non-linear, with integrated galaxy-formation efficiency peaking near a Milky-Way-scale halo of about 10^12 solar masses and falling steeply toward both lower and higher halo mass.

At z about 0 the peak integrated central-galaxy efficiency, defined as central stellar mass divided by the cosmic baryon allotment of the halo, remains below about 20 percent, meaning even the most efficient halos convert only a minority of their baryons into central stars.

The intrinsic scatter in central stellar mass at fixed halo mass above the pivot is small, generally below about 0.2 dex and often assumed lognormal, when inferred jointly from abundance, clustering, and lensing with measurement errors removed.

Halo-occupation-distribution and conditional-luminosity-function models require separate central and satellite occupation distributions to reproduce both galaxy abundance and scale-dependent clustering, with the one-halo to two-halo transition producing measurable departures from a single power law.

Subhalo abundance matching can reproduce galaxy abundance and clustering by rank-ordering galaxies against halos and subhalos using a chosen proxy with scatter, treating monotonicity, proxy choice, orphan handling, and stellar-mass systematics as assumptions.
In collisionless N-body simulations, dark-matter halo clustering depends on formation history and concentration at fixed halo mass, an effect known as halo assembly bias.

Whether galaxy occupation depends only on halo mass or whether galaxy properties are explicitly coupled to halo formation history or concentration, producing observable galaxy assembly bias, is unresolved, because halo masses and secondary properties are noisy and correlated and environment can mimic the signal, and ignoring it can bias mass-only cosmological inference.

The dominant origin of scatter in the stellar-to-halo mass relation is contested among halo merger and accretion history, concentration, spin, baryonic stochasticity, and residual measurement error, because the inferred intrinsic scatter depends on the deconvolution and on cross-correlated galaxy observables.
claims.debate_topic: Origin of stellar-to-halo mass relation scatter

claims.text: Which halo proxy best links galaxies to halos in abundance matching, whether present maximum circular velocity, peak velocity or mass, infall values, or compound concentration-sensitive proxies, is unresolved, because satellite stripping and disruption, numerical resolution, and orphan galaxies change small-scale clustering predictions.

The mechanism that quenches satellite galaxies, whether starvation and strangulation, ram-pressure stripping, tidal effects, or group preprocessing, is unresolved, because satellite demographics constrain a delayed-then-rapid quenching pattern, with delays of roughly 2-4 Gyr followed by rapid fading below about 0.8 Gyr for local massive satellites, better than they identify a unique physical cause.

The slope and scatter of the stellar-to-halo mass relation below the pivot and toward dwarf galaxies are uncertain, with steep abundance-matching extrapolation competing against broader, more scattered dwarf occupation and incomplete luminous samples, because ultra-faint completeness, reionization, tidal histories, and dynamical-mass conversion remain poorly constrained.

Because clustering, abundance, group catalogs, weak lensing, satellite dynamics, X-ray, and SZ constraints each carry different degeneracies, no method recovers a definition-independent halo mass, and whether dark-matter-only mass, profile, and bias calibrations remain adequate or must include baryonic contraction, expansion, and mass redistribution at survey precision is unresolved.
claims.debate_topic: Halo-mass inference method and baryonic modification
